newsitem.title: UK: British managers make post-election demands.
newsitem.headline: British managers make post-election demands.

text.p: British managers yearn for low inflation and public spending, a review of the taxation system and a more constructive approach to Europe, the Institute of Management said on Monday.

Launching what it called its pre-election manifesto, the Institute demanded a rigid inflation target of no more than three percent, prudent government spending and a public sector debt of no more than three percent of national income.
It also urged "a vigorous review of the taxation system" including an open debate about public spending priorities.

"Managers have a clear recipe for ensuring Britain's global competitiveness," said Roger Young, the Institute's director general. "It combines the ingredients of economic learning, lifetime learning and flexibility."

Prime Minister John Major is expected to call an election on May 1 and the opposition Labour Party, 20 points and more ahead in the polls, is positioned to take power. The Conservative government has a medium-term target of 2.5 percent year-on-year for underlying inflation, a goal that shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown has adopted.
Brown has also pledged to follow Conservative spending plans for the first two years of a Labour government and not to put up income tax for the lifetime of that government.
The Institute said Britain's attitude to Europe left something to be desired.
It called for full involvement over single currency negotiations, a referendum over whether Britain should sign up for a single currency and a full say in Social Chapter talks.

Both the Conservative and Labour parties are keeping their options open over European economic and monetary union, which is scheduled to start on January 1, 1999. But while Labour has said it would sign the Social Chapter, which guarantees minimum employment rights, the Conservatives have rejected it.

The Institute's "Manifesto for the Millennium" also looked for an overhaul of the education system, linking it more closely to employers and support for continuous development through a working lifetime.
